comments.text:
Good instinct to flag this. Based on how these proxies (jira-proxy.js, salesforce-proxy.js) are written, there are two concrete gaps
    relative to what you're hoping is already true:

    1. They're not actually localhost-only right now. They're started with http.createServer(...).listen(PORT, callback) — no host argument.
       Node's default when you omit the host is to bind 0.0.0.0, i.e. all network interfaces, not just the loopback interface. So as
       written, anything else on your LAN that can reach your machine's IP on that port could hit it — this isn't just a "hopefully"
       situation, it's actually open beyond localhost today. The fix is to pass the host explicitly: .listen(PORT, '127.0.0.1', callback).
    2. CORS is wide open: both set Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *, meaning any page loaded in the same browser — not just wigwag.html — can
       make a cross-origin fetch to http://localhost:8934/:8936 and pull data through it, if it can guess the endpoint shape (which isn't
       secret — it's public in this repo). That's a real vector even with correct localhost-only binding, since a malicious or compromised
       tab running in your own browser is still "local" from the proxy's point of view.

    Beyond fixing #1, a few things worth layering on:

    - Tighten CORS to the actual origin wigwag is served from instead of * — trickier if you open wigwag.html via file:// (origin comes
      through as null), but still narrows the surface for the common case of serving it over http.
    - A shared-secret header: have wigwag's Settings hold a token that gets sent on every proxy request, and have the proxy reject anything
      without it. This is the strongest single addition, because it defends against the "other local process/rogue tab" case that
      localhost-only binding alone doesn't cover — binding restricts network origin, not same-machine origin.
    - Minimize the exposure window: only run the proxy while you're actually linking things, then kill it, rather than leaving it up
      indefinitely.
    - One thing already done reasonably well: the startup/status logging only ever prints the auth mode (token / password-flow), never the
      actual credentials or fetched record contents — so at least nothing sensitive is landing in a terminal scrollback or log file by
      default.

    The localhost-binding fix (#1) is the one I'd treat as not-optional — it's a real, currently-open gap, not a hypothetical one.

Root-caused and fixed. startMerge() is the single real merge function every caller goes through, but the GitHub sync path (connectGithubRepo, pollGithubForRemoteChanges) never checked whether a fetched file's own declared projectId matched the project it was being merged into -- and both are async functions that never re-checked state.projectId after their awaits either. Switching projects while a connect/poll was still in flight could apply a stale result (the merge itself, sha/etag bookkeeping, sync status) to whatever project happened to be active by the time it resolved.

Confirmed via a git-stash A/B that this reproduces the real reported bug exactly: reverting just the fix leaks a synced project's full issue list into a brand-new blank project when the connect resolves mid-switch.

Two independent layers now in place: (1) startMerge() itself refuses to merge content whose own declared projectId doesn't match the active project (the one legitimate caller that deliberately merges a foreign-declared file after an explicit user confirm -- Apply update's mismatch dialog -- opts out via a new allowProjectMismatch flag); (2) connectGithubRepo/pollGithubForRemoteChanges/pushToGithub each capture their project id up front and re-check it after every await.

Landed as commit 42e1019, with two new regression tests in tests/github-sync.spec.js. Full suite passes (500/500, only the two pre-existing KNOWN GAP staleness tests show their usual soft-fail marker). Related to #43/#45 (same GitHub-sync area, same session).

I like the direction, but "notifications on change" is necessary and not sufficient — a few other pieces need to exist before conversations can actually live in tickets rather than just being logged there:

Notifications themselves — wigwag has no push/poll-to-user channel today; the GitHub sync layer polls GitHub, but nothing watches the local tracker and tells a human "something changed." You'd need either a lightweight watcher (desktop notification, email, Slack webhook) triggered off the signed-history append, or a digest/mention model so people aren't pinged on every field edit — just comments and @-mentions aimed at them.

@-mentions and a notion of "who's this comment for." Comments today are just history entries — nobody is addressed. Real conversation needs a way to say "this needs Thomas" vs "just a log entry," or every comment becomes a notification to everyone watching the issue.

Read/unread state per user. Otherwise every reopen of an issue looks unchanged-vs-new the same way, and conversation threads become unnavigable once they're more than a couple comments deep.

Faster round-trip than the current GitHub-sync path. Right now writes go through a push-debounce and conditional-polling pull cycle — fine for backlog grooming, way too laggy for back-and-forth conversation. Real-time-feeling chat needs either a much shorter poll interval or a proper push channel (websocket/SSE) rather than the current ETag-polling model.

Threading/reply structure, since comments are currently a flat append-only log — fine for a decision trail, less fine for "which of these three points are you responding to" once a conversation gets going.

I'd treat notifications as the trigger that makes this worth doing at all, but mentions + read state are what actually make it usable as a conversation medium rather than a fancy activity log.

You're right that email and key aren't entangled -- that's by design, and it's already written down in docs/FORMAT.md's 'Identity and signing' section: 'This is explicitly not a security boundary. The email is self-proclaimed, not verified by any authority... a lightweight who-did-this-and-was-it-tampered-with mechanism for collaborators who are basically trusting each other already.' The signature's real job is tamper-evidence (did this entry's content change after it was signed), not authentication (is this really that person).

Interesting finding: the docs (and a code comment in wigwag-core.js) already describe an intended answer to your exact question -- a TOFU (trust-on-first-use) identity store that remembers which pubkey an email used first, and flags a LATER import claiming the same email with a DIFFERENT key as 'a possible impersonation attempt'. But I checked, and it's not actually wired up anywhere -- verifyPayload() is imported into wigwag.html's Component class but never once called. So today, literally nothing checks key-per-email consistency at all; the docs describe a plan that was never implemented.

Given that gap, I'd actually caution against implementing TOFU exactly as documented, because of the exact scenario you raised: since multi-device use is common, and each device/browser generates its own key independently the first time it's opened, strict TOFU would false-positive constantly -- your own laptop and phone, both legitimately you, would look like 'impersonation' to each other the moment their data merges, since each device's local TOFU store only ever saw ITS OWN key as tom@lant.uk's 'first' one.

My recommendation: don't try to pin one key per email at all. Keep email as the human-facing attribution/grouping label (already true everywhere), and let pubKey mean 'which device/session produced this', full stop -- multiple legitimate keys per email is the normal case, not an anomaly to flag. If you want SOME visibility here later, I'd suggest something soft and informational rather than a security alarm -- e.g. a project could note 'tom@lant.uk has signed from 3 different keys' as a fact, not a warning -- but I wouldn't build even that without a concrete reason it'd help, given the doc's own explicit stance that this was never meant to resist a motivated adversary. Fixed: the Notification API's own `tag` option now dedupes this at the browser level -- new Notification(title, { body, tag: 'wigwag-mention-' + commentId }) in checkForNewMentions. Two independent fire attempts for the same comment (from two tabs racing, or a same-tab retry) share the same tag, so the OS replaces rather than stacks them -- only one visible notification ever, regardless of timing.

This is a different, narrower layer than NOTIFIED_MENTIONS_KEY (the existing localStorage-based 'have we told the user about this' set): that already prevents re-notifying about the same comment on a LATER poll, but it's a check-then-act read+write with no cross-tab locking, so two tabs polling independently (no leader election, by design) could both decide 'not yet notified' in the same race window before either writes back. The tag fix closes exactly that gap natively, without needing any actual cross-tab coordination/locking.

Covered by a new test in tests/mentions.spec.js asserting the tag is derived from the comment's own id, plus a direct simulation of a second near-simultaneous fire collapsing into the same notification. Full suite: 606/606 passing.

comments.author: claude@lant.uk
comments.text:
Investigated the current code (no PWA infra exists yet -- confirmed via search: no manifest.json, no service worker, no Push API/pushManager use anywhere in wigwag.html; notifications today are plain `new Notification()` calls that only fire while a tab is literally open, per the mention-notification work earlier this session). Two real paths, and they don't have the same "quickest" answer for the app-shell vs. the push part:

**Getting the app itself on your phone -- quick, ~PWA:**
Mobile-responsive UI (row list/detail, header, switcher sheets) already shipped in Phase 1, and GitHub sync already runs client-side against the existing OAuth proxy the same way on mobile as desktop -- no new backend needed for sync. The fast path is turning wigwag.html into an installable PWA: add a `manifest.json` + app icons + a minimal service worker (even just for offline-cache/installability, no push logic required yet), then "Add to Home Screen" on the phone. This needs no native toolchain at all, which matters because **this devcontainer has neither Android SDK nor Xcode** -- only the Linux desktop Rust/webkit2gtk toolchain for the existing Tauri build. That's genuinely a day-ish of work, not a big lift.

**Push notifications when the app isn't open -- the actually hard part, same difficulty either way:**
Today's notification mechanism requires an open, polling tab -- there's no server that knows when new tracker content lands except whichever client happens to be open. Real "notify me even when the app is closed" needs: a service worker + Web Push subscription (VAPID keys) + a server-side relay that watches the repo (e.g. a GitHub webhook receiver, similar in shape to `jira-proxy.js`/`salesforce-proxy.js`) and fans out push messages to subscribed devices. That's genuinely new backend infrastructure, not a wrapper choice -- and it's needed **regardless** of whether you go PWA or native.

One more real constraint: if your phone is an iPhone, Web Push only works for a PWA actually installed to the home screen (iOS 16.4+) -- it does not work in a plain Safari tab. Worth confirming which platform this is for.

**Tauri Mobile** (Tauri 2, which we already use, does support `ios init`/`android init`) would give true native push via platform channels, but doesn't remove the webhook-relay problem above, and adds real setup cost this environment doesn't have today: Xcode/Android Studio toolchains (a Dockerfile change + rebuild, and this container still couldn't run an iOS build without a macOS host), code signing, and an Apple Developer Program membership for anything beyond a 7-day free-provisioning install. For "quickest," it's a strictly bigger lift than PWA for the same amount of push-infra work.

**Recommendation:** start with the PWA path to get something installed on your phone fast, and treat "real push when closed" as a separate follow-up needing a small webhook-relay server -- worth its own issue once scoped, since it's new infrastructure rather than a UI tweak. Marking this Blocked pending your call on: (a) PWA vs. native as the wrapper, and (b) whether to scope the webhook-relay push work now or later, and which platform (iOS/Android) to prioritize.

comments.text:
Context: Tom asked in chat whether there's a nice way for PWAs to get updated -- this is that discussion, filed as a proper issue per his standing instruction to always file ideas/suggestions this way rather than leaving them in chat.

The problem isn't wigwag's service worker (sw.js) itself -- it's deliberately minimal, existing only to satisfy Web Push's requirement for a registered SW (self.skipWaiting() + clients.claim(), no fetch handler, no asset caching at all -- see sw.js's own header comment, added for #72). So there's no stale service-worker cache to bust.

The real cause is a well-known installed-PWA quirk on iOS/Android: tapping the home-screen icon often resumes the existing in-memory page instance instead of doing a fresh network load, so code changes sitting on the server never reach the app until something forces a real reload.

Recommended fix: a lightweight version check on the page's visibilitychange event. When the app comes back to the foreground, fetch a tiny version marker file with cache:'no-store'; if it differs from what's currently loaded, show a small non-intrusive 'Update available -- tap to reload' banner rather than reloading silently. Deliberately NOT a silent auto-reload -- wigwag has real local in-progress drafts (comment drafts, edit-in-progress cells, etc.) that a surprise reload would blow away, so surfacing it as a dismissible prompt the user acts on is the safer choice.

Sketch:
- A small static file (e.g. version.txt or version.json) containing a build identifier, updated whenever wigwag.html changes (could be a content hash, a timestamp, or a manually bumped version string).
- A visibilitychange listener (only when document.visibilityState becomes 'visible') that fetches that file with {cache: 'no-store'}, compares it against a copy embedded in the page at load time, and if different, sets a small piece of UI state to show the banner.
- Banner action just does location.reload() (a real network navigation, which will pick up the fresh wigwag.html).
- Should also fire once on initial load in case the version already drifted while the tab was closed, not just on later visibility changes.

Not started -- filed for triage/prioritization, not picked up as work yet.

Root cause (found while investigating an unrelated issue earlier, not yet fixed): measureTableOverflow() computes `overflows = (el.scrollHeight - currentSpacer) > (el.clientHeight + 1)`, where currentSpacer depends on the PREVIOUS render's own tableOverflow state -- a self-referential height measurement. In a narrow band near the threshold, this can genuinely oscillate: setting tableOverflow triggers a re-render, which changes currentSpacer, which flips the measurement back, which triggers another re-render, forever. Confirmed via a live repro at the time: a real React 'Maximum update depth exceeded' (error #185) loop, using a small imported project plus a couple of edits -- did NOT reproduce with the standard demo fixture's usual row count, so it's specifically tied to certain table-content heights landing in that narrow oscillation band.

Tom confirmed today (2026-09-07) he genuinely triggered this live, and it manifested as real fan/CPU load (though at the moment he checked Firefox's about:performance just now, no wigwag tab was actively spinning -- consistent with the loop only running while that specific narrow-band table height condition holds, not continuously).

Not fixed yet -- flagged instead of patched blind under time pressure, since measureTableOverflow's height-measurement logic is central to the table-overflow-indicator feature and touching it risks a real regression across the existing table-overflow test coverage. Needs someone to actually sit down with a reliable repro (a small imported project + a couple of edits, not the demo fixture) and redesign the measurement to not be self-referential -- e.g. comparing against the actual DOM's current scrollHeight/clientHeight directly each render rather than a value derived from the previous render's own state.

The wordmark logo (flagpole + red flag + white cutout square) is mathematically centered on the FLAG rectangle alone, but the black pole sits immediately to its left -- so the eye reads the pole+red as one dark mass on the left, making the pure-red strip on the right look thinner by comparison, even though the underlying math is symmetric within the flag itself.

Fix: shift the white cutout 2 units left (from x:18-34 to x:16-32, same 16x16 size, no other proportions touched) so it's centered on the WHOLE icon's width (pole included) rather than just the flag portion -- verified with a side-by-side render before touching wigwag.html. This only affects the wordmark logo (viewBox "0 0 48 62", the one with a pole) -- the plain square logo used for the favicon/PWA icons (viewBox "0 0 44 44", no pole) is unaffected and was already correctly centered.

Two occurrences in wigwag.html use this exact wordmark markup (the main app's top bar, and the "unknown project" cold-start screen's own top bar) -- fixing both identically.
